title: Fatty Acid Degradation: The β-Oxidation Spiral

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Why does a fatty acid carbon yield more ATP than a glucose carbon?
cards.back: Nearly every fatty acid carbon is CH₂, as electron-rich as a chain carbon can be. A glucose carbon (H–C–OH) already carries an oxygen, so it is partly oxidized before the cell starts.
cards.quote: A typical glucose carbon is H–C–OH: it already carries an oxygen, so glucose is partly oxidized before the cell starts.
cards.section: Why fat is the reserve: the electrons

cards.front: Gram for gram, why does stored depot fat hold roughly six times the energy of stored glycogen?
cards.back: Dry fat already holds more than twice the energy of dry carbohydrate (glucose's oxygens add weight, not fuel), and glycogen is stored with about twice its weight in water while fat is stored nearly dry.
cards.quote: glycogen is kept with about twice its weight in water, fat nearly dry, so gram for gram of stored depot fat holds roughly six times as much.
cards.section: Why fat is the reserve: the electrons

cards.front: In human fat cells during fasting or exercise, which hormones start lipolysis, and through what signal?
cards.back: Epinephrine and norepinephrine bind β-adrenergic receptors, raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A (PKA). Falling insulin takes the brake off.
cards.why: Textbooks also list glucagon, but its direct effect is small in human fat cells.
cards.quote: When you fast or exercise, epinephrine and norepinephrine bind β-adrenergic receptors (7-transmembrane receptors) on the fat cell
cards.section: Stage 1: Mobilization, unlocking the droplet

cards.front: A compound raises cAMP and activates PKA in both liver and fat cells. Predict what happens to glycogen and triacylglycerol stores.
cards.back: Both are broken down together. The same cAMP → PKA signal drives glycogen breakdown and adipose lipolysis.
cards.quote: It is the same cAMP → PKA signal that breaks down glycogen, so both storage depots empty together.
cards.section: Stage 1: Mobilization, unlocking the droplet

cards.front: Free fatty acids released from adipose travel in blood bound to {{c1::serum albumin}}.
cards.quote: These released free (nonesterified) fatty acids, not the fat you eat or the fat you store, are what travels in blood, bound to serum albumin.
cards.section: Stage 1: Mobilization, unlocking the droplet

cards.front: What happens to the glycerol released from triacylglycerol in adipose?
cards.back: It is water-soluble and goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase phosphorylates it so it can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
cards.quote: The glycerol is water-soluble and goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase phosphorylates it so it can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
cards.section: Stage 1: Mobilization, unlocking the droplet

cards.front: In adipose lipolysis, which lipase removes each of the three fatty acids, in order?
cards.back: ATGL: triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol. HSL (hormone-sensitive lipase): diacylglycerol to monoacylglycerol. Monoacylglycerol lipase: removes the last fatty acid.
cards.quote: In order, ATGL takes triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol, HSL takes that to monoacylglycerol, and monoacylglycerol lipase removes the last fatty acid.
cards.section: Inside the droplet: perilipin, CGI-58 and three lipases

cards.front: CGI-58, the activator perilipin releases for adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), is mutated. Predict the effect on fat handling.
cards.back: ATGL cannot be switched on, so the first fatty acid is not removed and fat accumulates in tissues that should not hold it: Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome.
cards.quote: When CGI-58 is mutated and ATGL cannot be switched on, fat accumulates in tissues that should not hold it: Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome.
cards.section: Inside the droplet: perilipin, CGI-58 and three lipases

cards.front: Acyl-CoA synthetase activates a fatty acid by splitting ATP to {{c1::AMP}} plus pyrophosphate, not to ADP.
cards.back: Hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate makes the step irreversible.
cards.quote: The reaction splits ATP to AMP plus pyrophosphate (PPᵢ), not to ADP, and hydrolysis of the PPᵢ makes the step irreversible.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: Fatty acid activation uses one ATP molecule. Why is it charged as 2 ATP in the yield ledger?
cards.back: Two high-energy phosphate bonds are broken: ATP → AMP + PPᵢ breaks one, and PPᵢ → 2 Pᵢ breaks the second.
cards.quote: ATP → AMP + PPᵢ breaks one, and PPᵢ → 2 Pᵢ breaks the second, so activation costs 2 ATP, not 1.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Give the three steps of the carnitine shuttle.
cards.back: CPT-I (outer membrane) swaps CoA for carnitine; a translocase carries acylcarnitine across the inner membrane; CPT-II inside regenerates acyl-CoA.
cards.quote: A translocase ferries the acylcarnitine across the inner membrane, and CPT-II inside regenerates acyl-CoA.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: CPT-I, the main control point for burning long-chain fatty acids, is inhibited by {{c1::malonyl-CoA}}, the first committed intermediate of fatty acid synthesis.
cards.quote: It is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the first committed intermediate of fatty acid synthesis.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: Why does it make sense that malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I?
cards.back: Malonyl-CoA is high while the cell is building fat. Shutting the import gate then keeps the cell from burning the fat it is busy making, avoiding a futile cycle.
cards.quote: while the cell is building fat, malonyl-CoA is high and the cell does not waste energy burning what it is busy making.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: A drug inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the enzyme that makes malonyl-CoA, in liver. Predict the effect on mitochondrial oxidation of long-chain fatty acids.
cards.back: Oxidation rises. Less malonyl-CoA means less inhibition of CPT-I, so more long-chain acyl groups enter the matrix.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, the main control point for long chains.
cards.quote: CPT-I is the main control point for burning long-chain fatty acids.
cards.section: Stage 2: Activation and the carnitine gate

cards.front: A liver preparation is given a CPT-I blocker, then supplied with either palmitate (C16) or a medium-chain fatty acid. Predict which one is still oxidized, and why.
cards.back: The medium-chain acid is still largely oxidized; palmitate oxidation falls. The carnitine gate is a long-chain checkpoint, and medium chains mostly cross into the matrix as free acids, most clearly in liver.
cards.quote: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids mostly cross into the matrix as free acids without the carnitine shuttle, most clearly in liver, and are activated to acyl-CoA inside.
cards.section: Chains that skip the shuttle

cards.front: Name the four reactions of one turn of beta-oxidation, in order, with the carrier each one uses.
cards.back: 1. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD → FADH₂). 2. Enoyl-CoA hydratase (water, no carrier). 3. 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD⁺ → NADH). 4. β-Ketothiolase (fresh CoA; releases acetyl-CoA).
cards.quote: Oxidize, hydrate, oxidize: a double bond, then an OH on carbon 3, then a ketone.
cards.section: Stage 3: Beta-oxidation, one cycle run again and again

cards.front: In beta-oxidation, why is the β-carbon (carbon 3) turned into a ketone before the chain is cut?
cards.back: A plain bond between CH₂ groups gives an enzyme nothing to grab. With a ketone at carbon 3, thiolase's cysteine attacks it, and the thioester steadies the negative charge left on carbon 2, so acetyl-CoA leaves.
cards.quote: a plain carbon–carbon bond between CH₂ groups gives an enzyme nothing to grab.
cards.section: Stage 3: Beta-oxidation, one cycle run again and again

cards.front: In beta-oxidation, why does the first oxidation use FAD while the second uses NAD⁺?
cards.back: Making a C=C double bond from two CH₂ groups releases too little energy to reduce NAD⁺, so the enzyme uses its tightly bound FAD. Oxidizing an alcohol to a ketone is a closer match for NAD⁺.
cards.why: Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD for the same reason.
cards.quote: Making a carbon–carbon double bond out of two CH₂ groups releases too little energy to push electrons onto NAD⁺
cards.section: Stage 3: Beta-oxidation, one cycle run again and again

cards.front: Which stretch of the citric acid cycle runs the same three moves as a beta-oxidation turn, and which of its enzymes matches acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in using FAD?
cards.back: Succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate: oxidize, hydrate, oxidize. Succinate dehydrogenase, like acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, forms a C=C double bond and hands the electrons to bound FAD.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that making a C=C from two CH₂ groups releases too little energy to reduce NAD⁺.
cards.quote: the citric acid cycle uses it to turn succinate into fumarate, then malate, then oxaloacetate.
cards.section: Stage 3: Beta-oxidation, one cycle run again and again

cards.front: Why is each FADH₂ from acyl-CoA dehydrogenase worth only about 1.5 ATP?
cards.back: Its electrons pass through electron-transferring flavoprotein (ETF) and ETF:ubiquinone oxidoreductase to ubiquinone, skipping complex I, like the FADH₂ of succinate dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: passes its electrons to ubiquinone through electron-transferring flavoprotein (ETF) and ETF:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, skipping complex I
cards.section: Where step 1's electrons go

cards.front: Where are very-long-chain fatty acids (about C22 and longer) first shortened, and why does that step make less ATP?
cards.back: In peroxisomes. There step 1 hands its electrons to O₂, making H₂O₂, instead of to the electron transport chain.
cards.quote: are first shortened in peroxisomes, where step 1 hands its electrons to O₂, making H₂O₂, so less ATP is made.
cards.section: Who does step 1 at each chain length

cards.front: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂ and 10 per acetyl-CoA, calculate the net ATP from fully oxidizing one palmitate (C16).
cards.back: 7 turns, 8 acetyl-CoA. 7 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 10.5; 7 NADH × 2.5 = 17.5; 8 × 10 = 80. Gross 108. Minus 2 for activation: about 106 ATP.
cards.quote: Gross: 28 + 80 = 108 ATP. Subtract the activation toll: 108 − 2 = 106 ATP
cards.section: The ledger: counting packets

cards.front: Myristate is a saturated C14 fatty acid. How many beta-oxidation turns, acetyl-CoA, FADH₂ and NADH does it give, and what is its net ATP (2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 10 per acetyl-CoA)?
cards.back: 6 turns, 7 acetyl-CoA, 6 FADH₂, 6 NADH. 6 × 4 = 24; 7 × 10 = 70; 94 − 2 activation = 92 ATP.
cards.why: Each turn makes one cut, so n pieces need n − 1 turns. Counting 7 turns is the common error.
cards.quote: Each turn makes one cut, and a ruler needs seven cuts to become eight pieces.
cards.section: The ledger: counting packets

cards.front: Stearate is a saturated C18 fatty acid. Calculate its net ATP (2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 10 per acetyl-CoA).
cards.back: 8 turns, 9 acetyl-CoA. 8 × (1.5 + 2.5) = 32; 9 × 10 = 90. Gross 122, minus 2 activation = 120 ATP.
cards.quote: stearate (C18, saturated) nets 120 ATP, oleate (C18, one cis bond at an odd-numbered position) 118.5
cards.section: Special cases that bend the rule

cards.front: Oleate (C18, one cis double bond at an odd-numbered position) nets 118.5 ATP versus 120 for stearate. What extra enzyme does it need, and why is it 1.5 ATP short?
cards.back: cis-Δ³-enoyl-CoA isomerase moves the bond to trans-Δ². The double bond is already there, so that turn skips the FAD step: one fewer FADH₂, worth about 1.5 ATP.
cards.quote: cis-Δ³-enoyl-CoA isomerase moves it to the trans-Δ² position and the cycle resumes.
cards.section: Special cases that bend the rule

cards.front: Glucose fully oxidized gives about 32 ATP and palmitate (C16) about 106. Compare their yields per carbon.
cards.back: Glucose: 32 / 6 ≈ 5.3 ATP per carbon. Palmitate: 106 / 16 ≈ 6.6 per carbon, about a quarter more. One palmitate is worth a little more than three glucose (106 / 32 ≈ 3.3).
cards.quote: Palmitate gives 106 from 16, about 6.6 per carbon: about a quarter more, and one palmitate is worth a little more than three glucose.
cards.section: The ledger: counting packets

cards.front: A child with MCAD (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase) deficiency skips breakfast during a stomach bug. Predict blood glucose and ketones, and explain.
cards.back: Glucose falls and ketones stay low: hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Every long chain becomes a medium chain on the way down, so much of fat burning stalls; too little acetyl-CoA reaches ketogenesis, and tissues burn glucose instead.
cards.why: The liver also loses the energy from fat it needs to make more.
cards.quote: Blood sugar falls without ketones appearing: hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
cards.section: MCAD deficiency: a block in the middle stalls the spiral

cards.front: A person eats unripe ackee fruit, whose hypoglycin A metabolite poisons several acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. Predict the fasting blood glucose and ketone pattern.
cards.back: By inference from the lesson (same step as MCAD, several dehydrogenases poisoned), expect low glucose with low ketones. A block at step 1 stalls beta-oxidation, so little acetyl-CoA reaches ketogenesis and tissues fall back on glucose.
cards.why: Rests on the MCAD rule: a block at step 1 gives hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
cards.quote: where a metabolite of hypoglycin A from unripe ackee fruit poisons several of the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases.
cards.section: MCAD deficiency: a block in the middle stalls the spiral

cards.front: What does the last thiolase cut of an odd-chain fatty acid leave, and what does it become?
cards.back: Propionyl-CoA (3 carbons). A biotin enzyme makes methylmalonyl-CoA, an epimerase flips it, and a vitamin B12 enzyme rearranges it to succinyl-CoA, a citric acid cycle intermediate.
cards.quote: The last thiolase cut leaves a three-carbon propionyl-CoA instead of an acetyl-CoA.
cards.section: Special cases that bend the rule

cards.front: A patient is deficient in vitamin B12. Predict a urine finding that traces to odd-chain fatty acid oxidation.
cards.back: Methylmalonic acid in urine. The B12 enzyme that rearranges methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA stalls, so methylmalonyl spills over.
cards.quote: A B12 deficiency stalls this step and spills methylmalonic acid into urine.
cards.section: Special cases that bend the rule

cards.front: Why can mammals not make net glucose from even-chain fatty acids by the usual route?
cards.back: Their carbons arrive only as acetyl-CoA. Each citric acid cycle turn brings in two carbons and loses two as CO₂, so no net oxaloacetate is left to seed gluconeogenesis.
cards.quote: Each turn of the citric acid cycle brings in two carbons as acetyl-CoA and loses two as CO₂, so no net oxaloacetate is left over to seed gluconeogenesis.
cards.section: Why even-chain fat gives no net glucose

cards.front: During a long fast, compare two triacylglycerols: one with three palmitate (C16) chains, one with a C17 chain among them. Which parts of each can give net glucose?
cards.back: Tripalmitin: only the glycerol backbone. The C17-containing fat: glycerol plus the three-carbon propionyl tail of the C17 chain, via succinyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. All other carbons leave as acetyl-CoA and give no net glucose, apart from a small trickle through acetone.
cards.why: Rests on the even-chain rule and the odd-chain route to succinyl-CoA.
cards.quote: only the odd-chain tail and the glycerol backbone make net sugar.
cards.section: Why even-chain fat gives no net glucose

cards.front: Why does the liver make ketone bodies when glucose is scarce?
cards.back: Low insulin floods the liver with fatty acids and opens CPT-I, so beta-oxidation makes acetyl-CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can burn it. Fasting raises HMGCS2, and oxaloacetate drawn off for gluconeogenesis adds to the surplus.
cards.quote: The liver's β-oxidation then makes acetyl-CoA faster than its citric acid cycle can burn it.
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: Which regulated enzyme commits acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies in the fasting liver?
cards.back: HMGCS2 (HMG-CoA synthase). Fasting signals raise its amount.
cards.quote: the regulated enzyme that commits acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: Acetoacetate is reduced to {{c1::D-3-hydroxybutyrate}}, the dominant ketone body in blood.
cards.quote: Thiolase, HMGCS2 and HMG-CoA lyase build acetoacetate, which is reduced to D-3-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant form in blood)
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: In diabetic ketoacidosis, what forms the fruity-smelling ketone on the breath, and how?
cards.back: Acetoacetate decarboxylates spontaneously to acetone, which is exhaled as fruity "acetone breath".
cards.quote: Acetone is exhaled as the fruity "acetone breath" that can get diabetic ketoacidosis mistaken for drunkenness.
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: Why can the liver not burn the ketone bodies it makes, and which cells also cannot use them?
cards.back: The liver lacks thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase), which reloads acetoacetate onto CoA to split it into two acetyl-CoA. Red blood cells cannot either: they have no mitochondria.
cards.quote: It lacks thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase), the enzyme that reloads acetoacetate onto CoA so it can be split back into two acetyl-CoA.
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: The liver oxidizes palmitate and exports its 8 acetyl-CoA as 4 acetoacetate. How much ATP does the liver keep, and how much do the tissues get (each reload onto CoA costs one GTP)?
cards.back: Liver keeps only the carriers: 7 × (1.5 + 2.5) − 2 = 26 ATP. Tissues: each acetoacetate gives 2 acetyl-CoA (20) minus 1 GTP = 19; 4 × 19 = 76.
cards.quote: If it exports palmitate's eight acetyl-CoA as four acetoacetate, it keeps 7 × 4 − 2 = 26 ATP, about a quarter of the 106.
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: The liver exports palmitate's carbon as 4 D-3-hydroxybutyrate instead of acetoacetate. Recalculate liver and tissue ATP, and explain why the total is not 106.
cards.back: Each ketone carries one liver NADH (2.5): liver 26 − 10 = 16, tissues 76 + 10 = 86. Total 102; the missing 4 are the four GTP the tissues spend reloading ketones onto CoA.
cards.quote: Liver plus tissues total 102, not 106; the missing 4 are the four GTP the tissues give up to reload the ketones onto CoA.
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: In George Cahill's starvation studies, daily protein breakdown was measured over a long fast. What did it show by day 40, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Protein breakdown fell from roughly 75 to about 20 grams a day. As the brain shifted onto ketone bodies, it needed less glucose made from amino acids, sparing muscle.
cards.quote: by day 40 of a fast, protein breakdown falls from roughly 75 to 20 grams a day as the brain shifts onto ketones
cards.section: Ketone bodies: the liver's fasting export

cards.front: In a long fast, fat stores are huge and muscle is precious. Why can the body not simply turn even-chain fat into glucose for the brain, and how does the liver solve the problem instead?
cards.back: Even-chain fat gives acetyl-CoA, which by the usual route yields no net glucose (only a small trickle via acetone), so early brain glucose comes mainly from glycerol and amino acids. The liver instead exports surplus acetyl-CoA as ketone bodies, which the adapted brain burns, sparing protein.
cards.why: Combines the even-chain rule with ketogenesis and Cahill's protein-sparing data.
cards.quote: mammals cannot make net glucose from even-chain fatty acids by the usual route.
cards.section: Why even-chain fat gives no net glucose

cards.front: A person on a β-adrenergic receptor blocker exercises. Can adipose lipolysis still be triggered by a hormone signal, and through what second messenger?
cards.back: Yes, in part. The catecholamine–cAMP route is blunted, but heart-derived natriuretic peptides can still start lipolysis through cGMP rather than cAMP.
cards.quote: heart-derived natriuretic peptides also start lipolysis, through cGMP rather than cAMP.
cards.section: A second route to lipolysis

cards.front: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin is high and the liver is building fat. Predict adipose lipolysis and liver mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, and give the control point for each.
cards.back: Both low. High insulin keeps the brake on adipose lipolysis (the cAMP–PKA route is not released). Fat synthesis keeps malonyl-CoA high, which shuts CPT-I, so long chains are not imported.
cards.why: Combines the hormonal control of mobilization with the malonyl-CoA gate.
cards.quote: raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A (PKA), while falling insulin takes the brake off.
cards.section: Stage 1: Mobilization, unlocking the droplet
